text: Cassini’s final dive wasn’t just an accident or running out of fuel, it was a planned ending. The spacecraft had orbited Saturn for years, so it may have carried tiny microbes or organic bits from Earth. If it had hit a moon like Enceladus or Titan, those residues could have landed on a surface that might be able to support life. By sending it into Saturn’s upper atmosphere, it breaks apart before it could crash into a moon, which keeps potentially habitable surfaces cleaner. There wasn’t a huge chance it would land on Enceladus, but the design was conservative.

I'm pretty sure your stationary leg is doing more than just hanging there, and it's acting like a counterweight and stabiliser while your active leg pushes and your upper body sways. On a skateboard, the foot you leave off the board has to keep the board level by subtly adjusting ankle and knee, and if you keep riding the same way, that dangling leg can build up fatigue, and the push side gets overused. So if the stationary leg is your left, your right leg is probably doing all the pushing, and the left is just sitting with the hip flexed or extended in a kind of awkward position for a long time. I think the pain usually comes from muscles getting tired, or joints getting loaded in a repetitive, off-balance way, not because the leg is completely inactive (this is why beginners get knee or hip ache after only a few rides). If you're on a longboard or cruising, the pain could be from holding the leg at an angle, and if it's your push leg that hurts, it's likely from too much pushing or pushing with bad form. Try shifting weight more evenly, shortening pushes, or alternating which leg you leave off for a session, and see if the pain eases, because often it's just muscle fatigue and imbalance rather than something seriously wrong. I’d say the name is about ancestry, not current residence, and that’s the key. 'African American' or 'Afro-American' points to heritage from Africa, mostly West and Central Africa, because the people in the US largely came through forced migration and slavery. So being called that doesn’t mean you were born in Africa, or even that you’ve ever lived there; it means your family roots reach back there. And for a lot of Black Americans, those roots are real, even if they’ve been in the US for generations. I think the confusion comes from the word 'American', which can sound like geography, but here it’s marking an ethnic and cultural identity. It’s less like a nationality and more like an ancestral label. So tbh the term isn’t claiming most Black people are from Africa today, it’s acknowledging where their forebears came from, and that’s why it’s used even for people with no personal connection to the continent. There’s also a reason it’s used in official categories: it groups people by shared history and identity, not by a birthplace. I’m pretty sure that’s why the label sticks even when individuals weren’t actually from Africa. It’s a heritage marker, not a travel record.

tbh, kind of, most Syrian weapons come from what they already had, what they captured, and what gets smuggled in from neighboring countries. So state arsenals, captured stocks from other sides, and black market flows through border routes are the main sources. They keep getting them because nobody fully trusts a ceasefire, and every side wants to be able to fight or defend. In Idlib, a fighter needs rifles, mortars, and sometimes heavy weapons. They buy or capture whatever works, even if it's worn out. There are local shops and warehouses along the Syrian-Turkish border used for transfers.

Hi Sam,

tbh this is pretty common, and it's real. When you spend hours walking and standing on shopping days, your body gets fatigued, dehydrated, and stressed, so you can get this dull pressure or headache-ish pain that feels different from a normal headache. It's mostly tiredness plus the sensory overload of crowds and lights, and sometimes your blood sugar or posture is off too. And it can hit you at the end of the day. Try drinking water, eating small meals, and taking a break when you start feeling it, and if it keeps happening, talk to your doctor. Hope that helps.

Cheers

Hey Sam,

I know you have a bunch of house-buying questions, and I can only answer the general ones because the list didn't come through clearly (maybe check if attachments sent?). So I'll just stick to the practical bits.

The first thing that helps is separating what you can afford from what you'll actually enjoy living with. Banks will quote a max, but your monthly budget is more realistic. A good rule of thumb is that housing costs, including taxes and insurance, should stay around 30% of take-home pay, and don't forget maintenance, which is usually estimated at 1% of property value per year.

Location matters more than the exact room layout, since you can renovate rooms but you can't change the neighbourhood. Walk to school, bus, and local shop before you commit. Also, never skip the building survey, it's the cheapest way to find expensive problems early. For a first-time buyer, check that the estate agent is registered, that searches are ordered, and that your solicitor is experienced with local property.

Also, if you have a deposit, see if you qualify for shared ownership or help-to-buy, and make sure the price includes any fixtures you assume are staying. If you can send the actual list, I can be more specific.

Cheers,
Alex

So the short version is that a 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner is a compromise formula. Individual products are tuned for one job. A normal bodywash uses surfactants and moisturizers for skin, shampoo targets hair cleansing, conditioner targets hair care, and each uses ingredients at concentrations suited to that single task. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner only needs to work on hair. A 3-in-1 has to do all of that and also clean the body, so the formula gets built around a wider mix of cleansing agents, conditioning agents and skin-safe humectants. And in practice it tends to be milder and less strongly lathering than dedicated products, so you get something that is okay everywhere but not great at any one job. (Which is exactly why most people who use it still reach for separate products later.) The big practical difference is that 3-in-1 spreads the ingredients across more uses, rather than optimizing for skin or hair alone. I’d say the 3-in-1 is less about doing three things really well and more about one bottle that won’t mess up either. If you’re only using it for travel or gym bags, that’s the whole point: it saves space but you trade some performance for convenience.

Cheers

Inbreeding doesn't mean the child will be low IQ, but the odds are higher, and that's the science bit. When parents share ancestors, their genes are more likely to be copies of the same variants. So the offspring inherit two copies of harmful recessive mutations more often, and the effect shows up as lower average cognitive scores. It's not one single gene; it's the build-up of many small effects plus rare harmful recessives becoming homozygous. The closer the relationship, the higher the inbreeding coefficient, and the bigger the expected drop. You can think of it like a genetic safety check that's skipped more often. That's why inbreeding is linked to lower IQ on average. And it's not just about looks or health; the same pattern also shows up in how the brain develops and works. In practice, even 1st cousins can show a measurable effect, though it varies a lot.

When someone is hit, shot, or stabbed in the arm, the pain is often lower than in the torso, legs, or hands. The main reason is nerve density. The arms, especially the upper arm and forearm, have fewer pain-sensing nerve endings compared with areas like the chest, abdomen, face, or palms. So the same force or object may trigger less pain signal. Muscle and skin matter too: a hit into muscle can feel duller than into bone, fascia, or dense tissue. The arm is also less involved in vital functions like breathing, which can make the injury feel less urgent. The brain also downplays pain when the area feels less threatening. That doesn’t mean arm injuries are safe. A bad cut, fracture, or nerve damage can still be very painful, and everyone’s pain threshold is different. In short, lower nerve density, tissue type, and perceived threat make arm injuries often seem less painful than injuries elsewhere.

So the short answer is that carbon monoxide sticks to the haemoglobin in your red blood cells way more strongly than oxygen does, which is the whole problem. And carbon dioxide doesn't really compete with oxygen in that same way. So CO effectively hijacks your oxygen transport, and your tissues start to starve even if there's plenty of oxygen in the air you're breathing.

I'm pretty sure the affinity is somewhere around 200 to 250 times stronger than oxygen, and that means even small amounts of CO in a room can seriously mess with how much oxygen actually gets to your brain and heart. But tbh CO2 isn't completely harmless either, it's just that your body is very good at getting rid of it (we exhale it every time we breathe out, which is the main way it leaves you). At very high levels CO2 can make you feel dizzy or short of breath, but in normal air it isn't the main culprit for this kind of poisoning.

And here's the annoying part: CO is colourless and odourless, so you often don't even notice it's there. That makes it much more dangerous than CO2, which you can sometimes sense as a kind of stuffy, heavy air. So in a wiki for a new colleague with no background, the key takeaway is that CO binds haemoglobin strongly and silently, while CO2 mostly just gets breathed out. If anything feels off in a sealed or poorly ventilated space, check for CO rather than assume it's just regular tiredness.

Before industrialization, businesses were mostly local and personal, so their names rarely survived. A craftsman, merchant, or family shop could be known in a town, but if the owner retired, moved on, or the trade declined, the name usually disappeared. Some old trading houses and monasteries did commerce, but they weren't the modern kind of company with mass production, national distribution, and recognizable branding. Industrialization changed things because factories, rail transport, and standard products let firms serve larger markets and persist across generations. So it's not that pre-industrial companies didn't exist; the idea of a famous, long-lived business really belongs to the industrial era.

When people tell me the dealer quote always looks better because the sticker rate is lower, I get it, but total cost is a different story. I take the position that financing at a bank is usually cheaper even if its APR is higher, because dealers tend to bury cost in the fine print and add-ons.

I remember walking into a showroom with a loan quote at 4.99% for 60 months. On paper that beats my bank's 6.25% for the same term. The dealer package included a $1,200 dealer prep fee, a $300 document fee, mandatory GAP insurance, and a 3-year maintenance plan. My bank had a $100 loan origination fee, but no required add-ons and I could pay it off early without penalty. The lower dealer rate didn't survive the add-ons and fees.

I think US states are doing the sensible thing by treating marijuana as a state policy choice, because 23 states plus DC have legalized it. The practical detail that matters is the gap between medical and recreational rules. A state can allow doctor-verified patients to grow 3 plants at home but still ban adult sale in stores. That split creates confusion: someone can legally cultivate for medical use while a neighboring state allows retail. So I’m in favor of states setting their own rules, but I’d push for clear, simple laws. If a state legalizes, it should spell out who can sell, how much people can possess, and whether home growing is allowed. The federal government treats it as a Schedule I drug, which leaves room for awkward overlap. In the end, state law is where the action is, and it’s enough for my family to plan a backyard patch.

I think the useful way to see it is that your body doesn't make electricity out of nothing; it moves charged atoms across membranes. Your cells keep potassium mostly inside and sodium mostly outside, mostly because of pumps that burn ATP. When a nerve fires, sodium channels open, sodium floods in, and the inside jumps from about -70 mV to roughly +40 mV for a moment. That brief flip is the signal. Muscles work on the same idea: calcium triggers contraction, but the membrane still runs on ion shifts. So biology is basically tiny batteries wired through a nervous system.

When I get a headache, I stop blaming my brain. My brain sits in a padded skull and doesn't really have pain receptors, so the hurt usually comes from the scalp, neck muscles, and reactive blood vessels. For me, tension makes my shoulders creep up to my ears and a tight band forms across my forehead, like a slow squeeze. The pressure makes me want to lie still in a dark room. I see it less as damage and more as an alarm. Stress, poor sleep, or dehydration make those muscles tighten and the vessels react, sending sharp, throbbing signals through the nerves. That's why my head hurts: the system is sounding a warning bell, not telling me the brain itself is breaking. I treat it as a message to slow down, stretch, drink water, and let the tension out before the alarm gets louder.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and tbh there was no line at all. Two people ended up paying about $130 which felt pretty steep. Before going I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse and after that I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one. And I was kind of disappointed that steak wasn’t offered because at that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws, and Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else so those were interesting. But the problem was there were no crab-claw crackers, and staff said wooden mallets were available but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us, so I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either and it kind of reminded me of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries but nothing really stood out, and they also had fresh juices although I didn’t try any. Overall I’d call the buffet acceptable but overpriced for what it offers, and if you’re curious it’s worth trying once especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long I’d probably reconsider.

So about 2 years ago we ordered 2 shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. The shirts never got to us because the sales rep wrote our address down wrong, and her handwritten 7 got read as a 1. We meant 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS shop to send it back, then it just vanished, and nobody ever said anything. We didn't find out for a few weeks. In the middle of the argument we ordered another 2 shirts. Rockmount wouldn't refund the first 2. The owner took over, and he admitted the shipment went to the wrong place, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He also said it was kind of our fault for not being nice enough to the people at 5401, who lived 4 doors away. So we challenged the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got a credit.
